Energy stored in a capacitor goes as the **square** of the charge, so a 21% rise in
energy means a 10% rise in charge.
**Step 1 — write the energy.**
U = Q²/(2C) ✓
so **U ∝ Q²** for a fixed capacitor.
**Step 2 — write the ratio of the two energies.**
U′/U = (Q + 2)²/Q²
= **1·21**
**Step 3 — take the square root.**
(Q + 2)/Q = √1·21
= **1·1**
**Step 4 — solve.**
Q + 2 = 1·1Q
0·1Q = 2
**Q = 20 C** ✓
**Why 21% and not 10%.** The examiner chose 21% because √1·21 = 1·1 exactly ✓ A 10%
increase in charge gives (1·1)² = 1·21, a **21%** increase in energy - the square law in
action.
**A check.**
original: U ∝ 20² = **400**
new: U ∝ 22² = **484**
increase: 84/400 = **21%** ✓ exactly as stated.
**Why energy grows faster than charge.** Each extra bit of charge must be pushed on
against the voltage already present ✓ The later charge costs more than the earlier, so
the total energy accumulates as Q².
**The three equivalent forms.**
U = Q²/2C = ½CV² = ½QV ✓
All three give the same number; which is most convenient depends on what is held fixed.
Here the **charge** changes and C is fixed, so the first form is the natural one.
**A caution.** If instead the **voltage** had been raised by 10%, the energy would also
rise by 21%, since U ∝ V² as well ✓ The square law applies to either variable, because
Q and V are proportional for a fixed capacitor.
**Reading the distractors.** **10 C** ✗ gives (12/10)² = 1·44, a 44% rise. **30 C** ✗
gives (32/30)² = 1·138, about 14%. **40 C** ✗ gives 1·10, about 10% ✓ Substituting each
candidate and computing the percentage rise tests them in one step.
∴ 20 C.

Find the equivalent capacitance from the charge, then solve the network for C.
**Step 1 — find the equivalent capacitance.**
C_eq = Q/V
= 0·75 x 10⁻³/10³
= 0·75 x 10⁻⁶ F
= **0·75 µF** ✓
**Step 2 — reduce the network.** Label the input terminal P and the output terminal Q.
Along the top, two 2 µF capacitors are in **series** from P to the top-right node N:
C_top = (2 x 2)/(2 + 2) = **1 µF** ✓
**Step 3 — find the two routes from N back to Q.**
through the diagonal: the capacitor **C** ✓
round the right and bottom: 2 µF in series with 2 µF = **1 µF** ✓
These two are in **parallel**, giving **C + 1** µF.
**Step 4 — put the two stages in series.**
C_eq = (1)(C + 1)/(1 + C + 1)
= **(C + 1)/(C + 2)**
**Step 5 — set this equal to 0·75 and solve.**
(C + 1)/(C + 2) = 0·75
C + 1 = 0·75C + 1·5
0·25C = 0·5
**C = 2 µF** ✓
**Step 6 — verify.** With C = 2:
C_eq = 3/4 = **0·75 µF** ✓
Q = 0·75 x 10⁻⁶ x 10³ = **0·75 mC** ✓ exactly the charge given.
**Why the answer must be around this size.** C_eq = (C + 1)/(C + 2) is always **less
than 1 µF**, approaching 1 as C grows large ✓ so 0·75 µF is comfortably within range,
and no very large or very small C is needed.
**The two rules used.**
**series**: 1/C_total = Σ1/C - the total is **smaller** than the smallest ✓
**parallel**: C_total = ΣC - the total is the **sum** ✓
Note these are the **opposite** way round from resistors, which is the usual source of
error in capacitor networks.
∴ 2.

"Passes undeflected" means the electric and magnetic forces **balance** - the condition
of a velocity selector.
**Step 1 — write the two forces.**
electric: F_E = **qE**
magnetic: F_B = **qvB**, since v̄ ⟂ B̄
With the fields mutually perpendicular and both perpendicular to the velocity, the two
forces act along the **same line** and can cancel ✓
**Step 2 — set them equal.**
qE = qvB
**E = vB** ✓ the charge cancels completely.
**Step 3 — substitute.**
E = (2 x 10³)(1·5)
= **3 x 10³ N C⁻¹** ✓
**Why the charge drops out.** Both forces are proportional to q ✓ so the balance holds
for **any** charge, positive or negative, large or small - the device selects by
**speed** alone, which is what makes it a velocity selector.
**The selected speed.** Rearranged,
**v = E/B** ✓
Only particles of exactly this speed pass straight through; faster ones are deflected by
the magnetic force, slower ones by the electric. A pair of slits then isolates a
monoenergetic beam.
**Where this is used.** In a **mass spectrometer**, a velocity selector first produces a
beam of known speed, after which a second magnetic field separates the ions by
**m/q** through r = mv/(qB) ✓ It was also the arrangement J. J. Thomson used to measure
the electron's specific charge.
**Checking the units.**
[vB] = (m s⁻¹)(T) = (m s⁻¹)(kg s⁻² A⁻¹) = **kg m s⁻³ A⁻¹** = **N C⁻¹** ✓ a field, as
required.
**Why the fields must be mutually perpendicular.** Only then are the two forces along
the same line and able to cancel ✓ If E and B were parallel, the magnetic force would be
perpendicular to the electric one and no cancellation would be possible.
**Reading the distractors.** **2 x 10³** ✗ is the speed itself, with no factor of B.
**1·5 x 10³** ✗ is the field B scaled. **1·33 x 10³** ✗ is v/B rather than vB - the ratio
inverted ✓
∴ 3 × 10³ NC⁻¹.

Doping adds **free carriers** but no net charge, because every added atom is itself
neutral.
**Step 1 — see what doping does.** An n-type semiconductor is made by adding
**pentavalent** atoms - phosphorus, arsenic or antimony - to silicon ✓ Four of the five
valence electrons form covalent bonds; the fifth is loosely bound and becomes a **free
electron**.
**Step 2 — count the charges in the donor atom.** A phosphorus atom has **15 protons**
and **15 electrons** ✓ It is **electrically neutral** before it is added and remains so
afterwards. Donating its fifth electron leaves behind a **positive ion** fixed in the
lattice - an immobile +e that exactly balances the mobile −e.
**Step 3 — conclude.** For every free electron there is a fixed positive donor ion, so
the crystal as a whole carries **no net charge** ✓ It is electrically neutral because
the **atoms** added were neutral.
**Why the other explanations fail.**
"**electrons are stationary**" ✗ - they are precisely the mobile carriers; without their
motion there would be no conduction.
"**electrons neutralise with holes**" ✗ - in n-type material holes are the **minority**
carriers, far too few to cancel the electrons. Some recombination occurs, but the
neutrality of the crystal does not depend on it.
"**mobility of electrons is extremely small**" ✗ - electron mobility in silicon is
about **1350 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹**, high enough to make n-type material the faster of the two ✓
**The charge balance written out.** Within any volume,
n (free electrons) ≈ N_D (donor ions) ✓
so the negative mobile charge and the positive fixed charge are equal and the net charge
is zero - the condition of **charge neutrality** that underlies all semiconductor
theory.
**The p-type mirror image.** Trivalent dopants such as boron create **holes**, leaving
behind fixed **negative** acceptor ions ✓ Again the crystal is neutral, for exactly the
same reason.
**Where neutrality does break down.** Only in the **depletion region** of a p-n junction,
where the mobile carriers have diffused away and the fixed ions are left uncovered ✓
That local imbalance is what produces the junction's built-in field.
∴ atom is electrically neutral.

The number of electrons is the total charge divided by the charge on one electron.
**Step 1 — convert the charge.**
1 nC = **1 x 10⁻⁹ C** ✓
**Step 2 — divide by the elementary charge.**
n = Q/e
= 1 x 10⁻⁹/(1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹)
= **6·25 x 10⁹** ✓
**Why charge comes in whole numbers of e.** Charge is **quantised**:
Q = ne, with n an integer ✓
There is no such thing as half an electron's charge in an isolated body. Millikan's
oil-drop experiment established this, and it is why the answer must be a whole number of
electrons.
**How small a nanocoulomb is.** A coulomb is an enormous charge - 6·25 x 10¹⁸
electrons ✓ A nanocoulomb is a billionth of that, yet still over **six billion**
electrons. Everyday static electricity involves charges of this order.
**Checking the arithmetic.**
10⁻⁹/1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹ = (1/1·6) x 10¹⁰ = 0·625 x 10¹⁰ = **6·25 x 10⁹** ✓
The division by 1·6 gives 0·625, and the exponents give 10¹⁰ - keeping those two steps
separate avoids the usual slip.
**A sense of scale.** A copper wire of 1 mm² cross-section contains about **8·5 x 10²²**
free electrons per cubic centimetre ✓ so the 6·25 x 10⁹ here is a minute fraction - a
charged body has only a tiny imbalance between its electrons and protons.
**The sign.** The body carries 1 nC of **charge**; if that charge is negative, it has
6·25 x 10⁹ **excess** electrons, and if positive, it is **short** of that many ✓ The
count is the same either way.
**Reading the distractors.** **1·6 x 10¹⁹** ✗ is 1/e, the number of electrons in one
**coulomb**, not one nanocoulomb. **6·25 x 10²⁷** ✗ and **6·25 x 10²⁸** ✗ have the
right mantissa with exponents astray by 10¹⁸ ✓ Checking the power of ten - 10⁻⁹ divided
by 10⁻¹⁹ gives 10¹⁰ - settles it.
∴ 6.25 × 10⁹.

Equal and opposite charges feel forces of the **same magnitude**, so the accelerations
differ only through the masses.
**Step 1 — write the force on each.** The charges are equal in magnitude, q, and the
field is the same E, so
F₁ = F₂ = **qE** ✓
(the directions are opposite, since the charges are, but the magnitudes match).
**Step 2 — write the accelerations.**
a₁ = qE/m₁ and a₂ = qE/m₂ ✓
**Step 3 — take the ratio.**
a₁/a₂ = m₂/m₁
= 1/(m₁/m₂)
= 1/0·5
= **2** ✓
**Why the ratio is inverted.** Acceleration is **inversely** proportional to mass for a
given force ✓ The **lighter** particle - here particle 1, at half the mass of particle
2 - accelerates **twice** as fast.
**A worked instance.** Take q = 1 C, E = 1 N C⁻¹, m₁ = 1 kg and m₂ = 2 kg:
a₁ = **1 m s⁻²**, a₂ = **0·5 m s⁻²**
ratio = **2** ✓
**What "through the same distance" tells us.** It is extra information, not needed for
the ratio of accelerations ✓ It would matter for comparing the **final speeds**: with
v² = 2as over the same s,
v₁/v₂ = √(a₁/a₂) = **√2** ✓
and the **times** would go as t = √(2s/a), giving t₁/t₂ = 1/√2.
**The kinetic energies gained, for contrast.**
KE = qEs for each ✓ **identical**, since both have the same charge magnitude and travel
the same distance in the same field. Equal energy, but the lighter particle carries it
as greater speed.
**Why the sign of the charge does not matter.** The two move in **opposite** directions,
but the question asks for the ratio of the **magnitudes** of the accelerations ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **0·5** ✗ is the mass ratio itself, with the inversion
forgotten - the commonest error. **1** ✗ would need equal masses ✓
∴ a₁/a₂ = 2.

Outside a uniformly charged conductor the field is the same as if **all the charge sat
at the centre**.
**Step 1 — check that the point is outside.** The sphere's radius is 2 cm and the point
is at 3 cm from the centre ✓ so it lies **outside** the conductor and the point-charge
formula applies.
**Step 2 — apply the formula.**
E = kQ/r²
with k = 9 x 10⁹ N m² C⁻², Q = 3 x 10⁻⁹ C and r = 0·03 m:
E = (9 x 10⁹)(3 x 10⁻⁹)/(0·03)²
**Step 3 — evaluate.**
numerator: 9 x 3 = **27**
denominator: (0·03)² = **9 x 10⁻⁴**
E = 27/(9 x 10⁻⁴)
= 3 x 10⁴
= **3 x 10⁴ V m⁻¹** ✓
**Why the charge may be treated as a point.** By **Gauss's law**, a spherically
symmetric charge distribution produces, outside itself, exactly the field of a point
charge at its centre ✓ The result holds for a solid or hollow sphere alike, provided
the charge is uniformly spread.
**What the field is inside.** For a **conductor**, the field inside is **zero** ✓ all
the charge resides on the surface and the interior is shielded - which is the principle
of the Faraday cage.
**The field at the surface, for comparison.** At r = 2 cm:
E = (9 x 10⁹)(3 x 10⁻⁹)/(0·02)² = 27/(4 x 10⁻⁴) = **6·75 x 10⁴ V m⁻¹** ✓
more than twice the value at 3 cm, as the inverse square demands: (3/2)² = 2·25, and
6·75/3 = 2·25 ✓
**Why the radius 2 cm appears in the problem at all.** Only to confirm that 3 cm is
**outside** ✓ Had the point been at 1 cm, the answer would be **zero**, not a scaled-down
field - a quite different question.
**Reading the distractors.** **3 V m⁻¹** ✗ and **3 x 10⁻⁴ V m⁻¹** ✗ are far too small -
they come from mishandling the powers of ten in 10⁹ x 10⁻⁹/10⁻⁴. **3 x 10⁶ V m⁻¹** ✗ is
a hundred times too large, from using r in centimetres ✓
∴ 3 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.

Adding charge to both spheres changes the **product** q₁q₂, and the force follows that
product.
**Step 1 — write the original force.**
F ∝ q₁q₂
= (+6)(+9)
= **+54** (in µC²) ✓
**Step 2 — find the new charges.** Each sphere receives −3 µC:
q₁′ = 6 − 3 = **+3 µC**
q₂′ = 9 − 3 = **+6 µC** ✓
**Step 3 — write the new force.**
F′ ∝ (3)(6)
= **18**
**Step 4 — take the ratio.**
F′/F = 18/54
= 1/3
**F′ = F/3** ✓
**Why the force is still repulsive.** Both charges remain **positive** after the
addition ✓ Had the added charge been larger - say −7 µC each - one sphere would become
negative and the force would turn to **attraction**.
**Why the distance drops out.** It is the same before and after, so r² cancels in the
ratio ✓ Only the product of the charges matters here.
**A check with actual numbers.** Taking d = 1 m:
F = (9 x 10⁹)(6 x 10⁻⁶)(9 x 10⁻⁶)/1 = **0·486 N**
F′ = (9 x 10⁹)(3 x 10⁻⁶)(6 x 10⁻⁶)/1 = **0·162 N** ✓
and 0·162/0·486 = **1/3** ✓ exactly.
**Why the force falls so much for a modest change.** The product falls from 54 to 18 -
by a factor of three - because **both** charges are reduced ✓ Reducing one alone, from 6
to 3, would have given only F/2.
**The general point.** Coulomb's law depends on the **product** of the charges, so a
proportional change in either multiplies the force ✓ Charges can be added or removed
freely by contact or induction, and the force responds immediately.
**Reading the distractors.** **F** ✗ assumes no change, though both charges have
altered. **3F** ✗ has the ratio inverted. **F/9** ✗ would need the product to fall
ninefold - which would happen if each charge were cut to a third, not reduced by
3 µC ✓
∴ F/3.
